paragraphs.heading: Patterns in the night sky
paragraphs.text: A constellation is a region of the celestial sphere where a group of visible stars seems to form a pattern or outline, often an animal, a figure from myth or an object. The stars in a constellation can look close together, but they usually sit at many different distances from Earth. Today the sky is fully divided up, so any point in a celestial coordinate system falls inside one of the modern constellations.

paragraphs.heading: Stories and wayfinding
paragraphs.text: The first constellations were probably defined in prehistory. People used them to tell stories of their beliefs and experiences, of creation and of myth. Different cultures and countries invented their own, and some of these lasted into the early 20th century. Giving constellations names also made it easier for astronomers and navigators to pick out stars.

paragraphs.heading: From Greece to the IAU
paragraphs.text: Western culture received its constellations through Greece, and they appear in the writings of Hesiod, Eudoxus and Aratus. Ptolemy, a Greco-Roman astronomer from Alexandria, listed the traditional 48 in his Almagest. Patterns for the far southern sky joined the list between the 15th and the mid-18th century, as European explorers sailed into the Southern Hemisphere. In 1922 the International Astronomical Union accepted the modern list of 88, each with a Latin name, and in 1928 it adopted official boundaries covering the whole celestial sphere.

paragraphs.heading: The zodiac
paragraphs.text: Twelve or thirteen ancient constellations make up the zodiac, which straddles the ecliptic, the path that the Sun, Moon and planets all cross. Where the zodiac came from is still uncertain, but its astrological divisions became prominent around 400 BC in Babylonian or Chaldean astronomy. Pisces, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer and Leo lie in the northern sky. Virgo, Libra, Scorpius, Sagittarius, Capricornus and Aquarius lie in the southern sky.

paragraphs.heading: Asterisms
paragraphs.text: Other star patterns, known as asterisms, do not count as formal constellations, but observers still use them to find their way around the night sky. An asterism can be a few stars inside one constellation, or it can share stars with more than one. The teapot in Sagittarius and the Big Dipper in Ursa Major are two examples.

paragraphs.heading: A sky that slowly changes
paragraphs.text: Where a constellation appears shifts through the year, because night on Earth falls at a slightly different point in its orbit around the Sun. A constellation that never sets below the horizon from a particular latitude is called circumpolar. Over far longer times the patterns themselves change, because each star has its own independent motion. Over tens or hundreds of thousands of years, well-known outlines will become unrecognizable, and astronomers can predict past and future shapes by measuring how individual stars move.
